groups.title: Observability
groups.question: Explain how you would know a Node.js service is healthy and find the cause when it is not.

followUps.Distributed Tracing with OpenTelemetry: How does distributed tracing help you debug a slow request that crosses several services?
followUps.Metrics & Health Checks: What should a health check verify, and what happens when a service has none?

evidence.text: A trace follows one request across services, with a span for each step and its timing.
Trace context is passed along in headers, so spans from different services connect into one picture.
You can then see which service or call made the request slow.

notEnough: Only naming OpenTelemetry without explaining what a trace shows.

evidence.text: Metrics like request rate, error rate and latency show how the service behaves over time.
A health check reports whether the service can do its job, for example whether it's up and can reach its database.
Without one, the platform keeps sending traffic to a broken instance and never restarts it.

notEnough: Only saying add health checks without saying what they check or why.

groups.title: Containerization
groups.question: Walk through how you package a Node.js app into a container for production.

followUps.Dockerizing a Node.js App: What does a multi-stage Dockerfile give you over a single-stage one?
followUps.Non-Root Users & Docker Security: Why should a Node.js container run as a non-root user?

evidence.text: A multi-stage build installs and builds in one stage and copies only the output and production dependencies into the final image.
The final image is smaller, faster to ship and has fewer tools and packages to attack.

notEnough: Only saying use multi-stage builds without saying what's left out.

evidence.text: By default a container's process runs as root.
If the app is compromised, a non-root user limits what the attacker can do inside the container and makes escaping harder.

notEnough: Only saying don't run as root without explaining why.

groups.title: CI/CD
groups.question: Explain how code goes from a git push to a deployable image in a CI/CD pipeline.

followUps.GitHub Actions for Node.js: What does a CI pipeline protect you from, and how do you keep it fast?
followUps.Container Registry & Image Tagging: Why should you tag images with the commit SHA instead of only using latest?

evidence.text: CI runs install, lint, tests and build on every push, so broken code is caught before it's merged or deployed.
Caching dependencies and running independent jobs in parallel keeps it fast.

notEnough: Only saying use CI without saying what it protects or how to keep it fast.

evidence.text: Tagging each image with the commit SHA ties it to the exact code it was built from.
latest moves with every build, so you can't tell what's running or roll back to an exact version.

notEnough: Only saying don't use latest without explaining why.

groups.title: Production Deployment
groups.question: Explain what you do to make a Node.js service safe to deploy and run in production.

followUps.Graceful Shutdown & SIGTERM Handling: Walk through what your service should do between receiving SIGTERM and exiting.
followUps.Environment-Specific Configuration: How do you keep development settings and credentials out of a production deployment?

evidence.text: On SIGTERM the service stops accepting new connections and fails its readiness check.
It lets in-flight requests and jobs finish, within a timeout.
Then it closes database and queue connections and exits.

notEnough: Only saying handle SIGTERM without the steps.

evidence.text: Each environment gets its own config and credentials from its environment variables or a secrets manager, not from files in the code.
Production credentials exist only in production, so dev settings and secrets can't leak into it, and the reverse.

notEnough: Only saying use environment variables without explaining separation between environments.
